title: Administrative Core - EPIC
text: Eukaryotic pathogens cause significant disease globally, and more locally, threaten the health of citizens in South Carolina and the Southeastern United States. Clemson University’s strength in eukaryotic pathogens research led the Clemson University Board of Trustees to approve formation of the Eukaryotic Pathogens Innovation Center (EPIC) in January 2013. The overarching theme of EPIC is the study of globally important eukaryotic pathogens using state-of-the-art molecular, cellular, biochemical, genetic, chemical, biophysical, and genomic approaches. The Specific Aims of the Administrative Core proposal are: (1) to continue building Clemson EPIC into a nationally and internationally recognized research center, (2) to recruit high quality faculty with diverse research interests to build critical mass and expand the breadth of EPIC, and (3) to develop and administer a comprehensive mentoring program to enhance Target Investigator (TI) success in research and grantsmanship. Three key approaches to achieving these aims are: (i) expanding the breadth of expertise by hiring additional faculty and postdoctoral researchers in the area of eukaryotic pathogenesis and providing them with comprehensive and intensive mentoring in research and grantsmanship to provide them with the tools to successfully compete for NIH R01 or equivalent funding; (ii) continuing to host presentations by top researchers in the field at the Cellular Biology of Eukaryotic Pathogens meeting and at Center/Departmental/College seminars to raise EPIC’s profile; and (iii) enhancing research infrastructure within EPIC and the Clemson Light Imaging Facility and the Clemson University Genomics and Bioinformatics core facilities to aid in the research enterprise. The overall plan for the EPIC Administrative Core combined with the demonstrated commitment of the College of Science and the Clemson University Administration will position EPIC to truly achieve the status of a Center for Biomedical Research Excellence.

title: Metabolic mechanisms of glioma progression
text:
To address the urgent need for new insights into the biological processes that promote glioma, the most
common type of malignant brain tumor, we measured metabolite levels in a collection of human glioma
samples and non-cancerous brain tissues. We identified a metabolite that is highly enriched in aggressive
gliomas and we now seek to reveal how it accumulates in these tumors and the role it may play in promoting
interactions between glioma cells and neurons. Because interactions between glioma cells and neurons are
known to be critical for brain tumor growth, our work may deepen our understanding of these interactions and
inform new approaches to treat glioma.

title: The Development of antigent-presentation modulating nanoparticles (APM-NPs) to improve immunization
text:
This study aims to engineer T cell responses via novel antigen-presentation modulating nanoparticles (APM-
NPs) with antigen presenting cell and tumor specificity that can enhance antigen presentation and potentiate
antigen specific T cell responses. To validate this approach, we will investigate the applicability of this platform
technology to generate a pro-inflammatory tumor microenvironment and treat cancer in mouse models.
Successful completion of this project will lay the foundational groundwork for a novel platform technology to
genetically modulate antigen presentation and enhance vaccination strategies, with applications to cancer,
infectious disease, autoimmunity, and beyond.

title: Collaborative Integration of HCV Molecular Virology and Mathematical Modeling
text:
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a hepatotropic virus that establishes chronic infection in ~70% of those exposed. While
effective direct acting antiviral (DAA) therapeutic combinations are highly potent, we are not yet on track to
achieve the WHO goal of elimination by 2030, which will require a scaling-up of HCV screening, linkage-to-care,
reduction of treatment cost as well as advancing our understanding HCV persistence and drug resistance.
Importantly, because viral cell-to-cell spread has been implicated in antiviral escape, immune escape, and
persistence of viruses in general, the insights gained through the proposed HCV studies should broadly inform
future antiviral strategies for hepatitis C and related viruses.

title: Interpretable and Adaptable Graph Neural Networks: Modeling Metapopulation Dynamics of Childhood Infections
text:
Despite decades of theoretical and empirical work, the problem of fully understanding and accurately predicting
the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of childhood infections, in the context of evolving public health
preventive and management strategies, remains unresolved. The key to a solution lies in enabling a deep
understanding of the intricate geometry of infection spread among a network of spatially interconnected
populations (i.e., a metapopulation). This project develops a new modeling framework—effectively combining
the strengths of mechanistic models and graph neural networks—to provide such a solution that is also key for
guiding effective prevention and management strategies for current and emerging childhood infections.

title: Towards an etiological model of adolescent eating disorders through neuroimaging, genetics, and behavior
text:
Eating disorders, including anorexia/bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder, have their peak onset during
adolescence but their etiological underpinnings are still largely unknown, leading to poor treatment outcomes
and even mortality. This study will be the first to prospectively study the genetic, neuroimaging and behavioral
factors that precede onset of an eating disorder in adolescence using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive
Development (ABCD) Study, as well as integrating independently collected clinical data to examine how
putative premorbid factors translate to clinical outcomes. Infusing a neurobiological perspective to an
etiological model of eating disorders will offer valuable directions for future treatment plans and clinical
assessments early in the course of illness.

title: Dysregulated genome architecture in acute myeloid leukemia
text:
Changes in DNA methylation and gene expression are hallmarks of acute myeloid leukemia, but mechanisms
underlying these changes are poorly understood. We propose to define the genome-wide relationship between
DNA hypermethylation and 3D genome architecture using primary AML samples with canonical DNA
methylation phenotypes, and to perform detailed mechanistic studies of epigenetic modifications, chromatin
interactions, and gene expression at the HOXA locus in primary AML samples and AML cell line models.
Together these studies should allow us to better identify genes that are dysregulated by the effects of DNA
hypermethylation, and may lead to new approaches for disrupting HOXA-mediated self-renewal in AML cells.

title: AI-Enhanced Perfusion MRI for Optimizing Y90 Particle Density in Radioembolization of Liver Cancer
text:
Radioembolization has become a viable treatment option for unresectable primary or secondary liver cancer.
However, significant challenges remain in providing personalized dosimetry that accounts for the altered
perfusion of primary or secondary liver cancer compared to normal liver parenchyma. In this project, we use a
combination of artificial intelligence and MR perfusion imaging to build a perfusion biomarker that interventional
oncologists can use to improve personalized dosimetry for radioembolization.

title: Center for Transformative Infectious Disease Research (CTIDR)
text: PROJECT 1 PROJECT DESCRIPTION Our proposed studies will investigate how extreme weather events and seasonal changes affect risk of spillover of zoonotic infections from bats. Our work will help identify evidence-based strategies to prevent disease emergence in multiple ecological settings. Bats are the known or progenitor hosts of four of the nine diseases identified by the World Health Organization as research priorities. Bats also may be exquisitely vulnerable to changes in weather because their food resources are seasonal and physiologically they are sensitive to temperature changes. We will leverage two long-running datasets on emerging pathogens from bat hosts to examine the role of weather in driving shedding patterns and spatial behavior of bats and likelihood of exposures in humans. Our methods, innovative both conceptually and methodologically, will use already collected datasets. We will integrate these datasets to move beyond assumptionladen correlations of spillover risk towards mechanistic understanding of how ecological, environmental, and host-viral drivers of infections influence disease emergence. Our work sets the stage for remote sensing methods to identify places and periods to prioritize for prevention of spillover. In Aim 1, we will identify weather-driven effects on the health of bats, diet, and paramyxo- and corona-, virus infection dynamics in Australia, using retrospective data collected previously by the PI. Hypothesis: We will observe higher prevalence of viral shedding in sampled bats after or during specific environmental conditions (e.g., hot, dry, then wet conditions, flood, high rainfall) and higher prevalence will be correlated to markers of bat health, diet and viral infection dynamics. We will use novel Bayesian multilevel models to analyze these data. In Aim 2: we will investigate how host space-use changes in relation to environmentally-driven resource availability and how these changes drive spatial and temporal overlap of bats and humans. Hypothesis: resource constraints on natural food sources will lead to increased contact between bats, humans, and bridging hosts. Our work will lead to strategies, derived from empirical data and modeling, that can help prevent spillover of pathogens from bats to humans. Preventing spillovers from bats in any part of the world reduces the risk of pandemics and reduces human mortality and morbidity in the United States; prevention of spillover is highly cost- effective when strategies are successful, and can lead to interventions that buffer effects of environmental change on sensitive species such as bats.

title: Models and Gene Therapies for AAT Deficiency-Admin Core
text: Project Summary / Abstract - Administrative Core The overarching goal of this application is to advance more efficacious and safer adeno- associated virus (AAV) gene therapy and base editing for single gene disorders, of which alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is among the most common. As we continue to progress in AAT gene therapy, we aim to address some fundamental limitations of these therapies. These include improving our understanding of the mechanisms of acute toxicity with very high intravenous doses of adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors, guiding our management of adaptive immunity to AAV and CRISPR components, optimizing AAV vector potency, and refining the performance of base editors that are highly compact precise and efficient. Since this program project entails multiple different modalities of gene transfer, gene editing and immune modulation, it will require a close coordination among the PIs of the 4 research projects and the 2 scientific cores. This administrative core serves to facilitate the work of the other 6 components through accurate and transparent cost accounting, the organization of regular recurring collaborative data meetings and the organization of internal and external peer reviewers to give input into our research direction and methods. Other administrative and logistical details will be handled through this core, enabling the PIs to focus on their science.

title: Administrative Supplement: Research Continuity Following Caregiving Responsibilities (R21AG087299)
text:
This supplement will provide short-term support to ensure continuity of an NIH-funded Alzheimer's disease
research project. Additional scientific personnel will accelerate analytic pipelines, develop methodology, and
assist with dissemination of findings. The work will advance public health by identifying biological pathways that
protect against Alzheimer's disease and supporting the development of strategies for prevention and treatment.

title: Defining bioactivities of peptides released from human milk proteins in the preterm infant intestine
text:
This project is relevant to public health and the mission of NICHD because it will help to characterize the function
of human milk beyond nutrition by identifying milk protein-derived bioactive peptides released within the gut of
preterm infants with gut health-promoting functions. Understanding the roles and identities of these bioactive
peptides will contribute significantly to understanding the benefits of human milk to infant health and how to
maximize those benefits to promote the healthy development of preterm infants. This proposal specifically
addresses two of the NICHD Pediatric Growth and Nutrition Branch's Research Priorities:1) Human Milk
Composition and Function (particularly how human milk composition changes with digestion and interacts with
the infant intestine), and 2) Nutrition for Preterm Infants (particularly understanding the role of bioactive
components of human milk (e.g., peptides) in feeding preterm infants).

title: Evolutionary Human Genomics: Demography, Natural Selection, and Transcriptional Regulation
text:
Vast quantities of genomic data are now available to describe patterns of genetic variation and gene
expression both within human populations and across species. These data need to be interpreted in
light of the fundamental forces of mutation, recombination, natural selection, and genetic drift that have
shaped our genomes over millions of years of evolution. This proposal describes a series of projects
that make use of new computational methods to address fundamental questions in human evolutionary
genomics, including how human diversity has been shaped by introgression from our archaic hominin
cousins, how new mutations influence human health and fitness, and how the evolution of gene
expression contributes to unique aspects of human biology and disease.

title: Integrative Approach to Comprehensive Analysis of High Throughput Data on a Cancer Center Level
text:
The application is aimed to support cancer-related research efforts of The Wistar Institute investigators through
computational expertise provided by Bioinformatics Shared Resource. The focus of the supported projects
involve experiments designed to understand basic mechanisms of cancers, including melanoma, ovarian,
prostate, various blood cancers, lung, colon, and many others, with the final goal of developing methods for
cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.

title: Transforming Mammography With STARLIGHT, Imagine Scientific's Monochromatic X-Ray Imaging System
text:
Transforming Mammography With STARLIGHT
Imagine Scientific's Monochromatic X-Ray Imaging System
Project Narrative
 Imagine Scientific has invented the first and only practical, IP-protected, cost effective,
high power, monochromatic X-ray source with short exposure times for diagnostic imaging in the
clinic. This long-awaited breakthrough for radiology is called STARLIGHT, which provides an
extensive range of selectable monochromatic energies with sufficient intensity and beam
coverage for many radiological imaging procedures. Its initial application for commercial
development is as an X-ray source for mammography. STARLIGHT offers (i) superior detection
of tumors for all women, including those with thick and dense breasts, (ii) significantly lower
radiation dose, and (iii) elimination of painful breast compression during examinations. In Year 1,
we intend to finish the commercial development and fabrication of the advanced STARLIGHT
source, and together with collaborators from the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) and the
University of California at San Diego (UCSD) in Year 2, conduct a clinical trial at Duke University
Medical Center to demonstrate specific and important clinical benefits of monochromatic imaging.

title: The Role of Annexin A1 Expression in Glioblastoma-Associated Astrocytes
text:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most lethal type of cancer that develops in the brain. While other brain cancers can
respond to immunotherapy treatments, immunotherapies do little to slow GBM’s growth. Researchers are
seeking novel strategies to activate the immune system against this devastating cancer. Astrocytes are one of
the most abundant types of brain cell that can activate or suppress immune responses. Critically, astrocytes
change dramatically, and potentially permanently, in response to environmental toxins and traumatic brain injury.
GBM is the third most common cause of cancer death in US active-duty military, GBM incidence is increased
among Veterans, and survival among Veterans with GBM is significantly shorter than non-Veterans. Reasons
for poorer outcomes in Veterans are unknown. This research investigates immune-suppressive GBM-associated
astrocytes using mouse models, clinical data, and GBM tissue from Veterans. Targeting immune suppressive
functions in astrocytes in Veteran GBM might improve immunotherapy responses, survival, and quality of life.

title: HIV Tat-associated Sensory Neuropathy and the Contribution of Toll-like Receptor Pathway
text:
“Improve HIV-related health outcomes of people with HIV” is one of the 4 goals identified in the recently
published US National HIV/AIDS Strategy (2022-2025), which involves addressing HIV-associated
comorbidities. HIV-associated sensory neuropathy (HIV-SN) is one of the most common neurological
complications associated with HIV infection, often painful, and clinically hard to manage. Studies investigating
the underlying mechanisms of HIV-SN, and help identify affordable treatment strategies are critical for
achieving the national vison for HIV/AIDS “… every person with HIV has high-quality care and treatment,…and
can achieve their full potential for health and well-being across the lifespan”.

title: GABAergic Circuit Targets for Modulating Entorhinal Cortex and Hippocampal Dynamics in Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) currently has no cure, and approximately one-eighth of Americans over 65
suffer from progressive memory and cognitive decline due to this debilitating brain disorder.
Our study aims to set the groundwork for possible new therapies by investigating specific brain circuits
vulnerable in early AD. Using mouse models and samples from human patients, our study will identify
brain cells that are affected versus remain resilient in early AD and evaluate how they can be engaged via
translatable neuromodulatory strategies to improve brain circuit activity and memory function and prevent
AD-related cognitive deficits before they manifest.

title: Neuroimaging Sciences Training Program
text:
The Neuroimaging Sciences Training Program (NISTP) combines expertise in brain imaging technology with
skill and knowledge in clinical applications to addiction for cross-training of postdoctoral trainees. The goal is
to foster the development of interdisciplinary scientists who can comfortably apply complex imaging methods to
understand the neuroscience of misuse and dependence of cocaine, opiate, nicotine, alcohol, and other
substances, as well as treatments for these problems.

title: Uncovering cargo and cell type specific molecular mechanisms of renal tubular epithelial transport
text:
Mutations in MYH9 that encodes for Nonmuscle Myosin IIA (NM2A), an actin
associated motor protein, have been associated with kidney disease in humans, but the mechanisms by which
MYH9 mutations cause kidney disease is unclear. Previous work focused on podocyte actin cytoskeleton in the
Glomerulus. Our recent work established a novel function for Myh9&10 proteins in cargo transport in the thick
ascending limb (TAL) epithelium, and loss of this function in mice resulted in rapidly progressing kidney disease.
We propose to investigate the role of Myh9&10 in the TAL cargo transport system in the kidney. We will also test
if combined loss of Myh9 protein in podocyte as well as tubular epithelium will lead to exacerbated disease due
to synergistic functional loss in both cell types. Our work will directly address the loss of distinct functions of
Myh9 in two different cell types within the kidney, reasonably modeling a severe form of MYH9-RD with complete
loss of function.
